Benchmark & method · adaptive driver alerting · CoRL 2026

VLAlertObserve Before You Alert: Adaptive Driver Alerting with Vision–Language Models

A unified per-tick benchmark for deciding when a driving system should stay SILENT, OBSERVE, or ALERT — and a vision–language policy in which the OBSERVE action acts as an internal evidence-gathering decision that delays uncertain warnings.

At each one-second tick a model sees the last eight frames and predicts the appropriate alert action. VLAlert-Bench joins six driving-event sources into one task — 13,534 videos and 192,892 labelled ticks across five splits — and the VLAlert policy, built on Qwen3-VL-4B, is scored on it and on held-out ADAS-TO-Critic takeover clips.

The paper's abstract describes VLAlert-Bench as built from four real-world dashcam alert datasets; the released card adds the ADAS-TO-Critic and Kaggle ACCIDENT extra splits, bringing the sources to six.

01 · OVERVIEW

When is the evidence enough to warn?

The arXiv abstract, verbatim, beside what you need to know at a glance.

Driver alerting from dashcam video requires sequential decision-making under partial observability: a system must decide not only whether a scene is risky, but also when the evidence is sufficient to warn. Most existing accident anticipation models output a binary risk score, leaving ambiguous scenes to be handled by thresholding. We propose VLAlert, a vision-language alerting framework that casts warning generation as a tri-action policy over SILENT, OBSERVE, and ALERT. The OBSERVE action acts as an internal evidence-gathering decision that delays uncertain warnings and changes the next observation window, creating a lightweight perception-action loop for adaptive alerting. VLAlert uses Qwen3-VL-4B as a safety-evidence generator and pools hidden states from structured belief spans to form compact representations for danger estimation and policy prediction. We evaluate VLAlert on VLAlert-Bench, a unified per-tick benchmark from four real-world dashcam alert datasets, and further test transfer to held-out naturalistic ADAS takeover clips. On VLAlert-Bench validation, VLAlert achieves the highest deployment-oriented utility among tested baselines, with DAUS 0.4878 compared with 0.4752 for Open-BADAS, and improves AUROC, AP_tick, F1_t, and balanced accuracy from 0.610, 0.176, 0.276, and 0.581 to 0.689, 0.195, 0.297, and 0.648, respectively. On 221 held-out ADAS-TO-Critic clips, VLAlert improves R@5s from 74.2% to 88.7% and F1 from 0.585 to 0.686. These results indicate that adaptive observation and safety-focused VLM representations provide measurable gains for driver-facing alert decisions.

03 · EVIDENCE

What the numbers rest on

0.4878 DAUS · Open-BADAS 0.4752

Deployment-oriented utility is where the tri-action policy pays off.

On VLAlert-Bench validation, VLAlert achieves the highest deployment-oriented utility among tested baselines — DAUS 0.4878 against 0.4752 for Open-BADAS; DAUS scores the usefulness of the alert stream rather than frame-level accuracy alone.

.689 AUROC · from .610

Four frame-level metrics move together.

AUROC .610 → .689, APtick .176 → .195, F1t .276 → .297, balanced accuracy .581 → .648.

88.7 % R@5s · from 74.2 %

It transfers to the lab's own takeover clips.

On 221 held-out ADAS-TO-Critic clips — naturalistic Level-2 takeovers recorded by the lab, not web uploads — recall within five seconds rises from 74.2 % to 88.7 % and F1 from .585 to .686.

192,892 ticks · five splits · six sources

One per-tick task over six event datasets.

A tick is a 1-second sliding-window record carrying 8 consecutive frame indices plus the action label at the window's last frame. The two extra splits — ADAS-TO (lab-recorded takeovers) and the Kaggle ACCIDENT challenge — are held out of training.
